No more forking Tree-sitter grammars.
Powderworks provides professionally maintained, well-tested Tree-sitter compatible Wasm grammars for security and code analysis, with comprehensive coverage of all the languages you care about.
The Tree-sitter ecosystem is great for editors. Its grammars are fast, incremental, and forgiving: they keep highlighting while you type and patch over code they don't understand. Static analysis needs something else. A SAST tool has to read every file the way the language's own tooling does, in the language version the project actually uses, and a grammar that patches or skips over code it doesn't understand means missed findings and false alarms.
So teams fork. When a grammar doesn't know a new syntax or a dialect your customers write, you patch your own copy and wait, hoping that the next upstream release will happen sometime this year and address your issue. Our goal is to end the forking: grammars for every programming language, for every version and dialect of each, all continually updated, maintained, and tested.
Our grammars are Tree-sitter compatible WebAssembly modules. They load into web-tree-sitter like any other grammar, and your queries, cursors, and bindings work just as they do with grammars Tree-sitter generates. They're the same parsers that power
Ur
.

One grammar per version
The same line of code can be valid in one version of a language and an error in the next. Our Python 2.7, 3.8, and 3.12 grammars read these three lines differently:
Code
2.7
3.8
3.12
print "hello"
✅
Error
Error
if (n := 10) > 5: pass
Error
✅
✅
match command:
case _: pass
Error
Error
✅
A single grammar for every version gets some of these wrong whichever version your project uses, and the scanner, linter, or migration tool built on it misreads your code. Pick the grammar for the version you target: it parses what that version parses, and returns a file the version rejects as one parse error, not a guessed tree. Dialects work the same way: PostgreSQL's
DISTINCT ON
parses in our PostgreSQL grammars and fails in our MySQL grammars.
Tested and maintained
We test each grammar against its language's reference parser on large real-world codebases, and check each Tree-sitter grammar against Ur's own trees, node for node. We maintain them continuously and fix the bugs you report promptly. Every grammar must parse all the real-world code we test it on, node for node and field for field.
